{{about|a concept in category theory|the concept in cognitive psychology and philosophy|prototype theory}}

{{Refimprove|date=April 2015}}

In [[mathematics]], if <math>\mathcal{A}</math> is a [[category (mathematics)|category]], then a '''<math>\mathcal{A}</math>-graded category''' is a category <math>\mathcal{C}</math> together with a [[functor]]
<math>F\colon\mathcal{C} \rightarrow \mathcal{A}</math>.

[[Monoid]]s and [[group (mathematics)|group]]s can be thought of as categories with a single [[object (category theory)|object]]. A monoid-graded or group-graded category is therefore one in which to each [[morphism]] is attached an element of a given monoid (resp. group), its grade. This must be compatible with composition, in the sense that compositions have the product grade.

==Definition==

There are various different definitions of a graded category, up to the most abstract one given above.  A more concrete definition of a graded [[abelian category]] is as follows:<ref>{{cite journal|last=Zhang|first=James J.|title=Twisted graded algebras and equivalences of graded categories|journal=[[Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society]]|date=1 March 1996|volume=s3-72|issue=2|pages=281–311|doi=10.1112/plms/s3-72.2.281|mr=1367080|url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/135651/1/plms0281.pdf|hdl=2027.42/135651|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Let <math>\mathcal{C}</math> be an abelian category and <math>G</math> a monoid.  Let <math>\mathcal{S} = \{ S_g : g \in G \}</math> be a set of functors from <math>\mathcal{C}</math> to itself.  If

* <math>S_1</math> is the [[identity functor]] on <math>\mathcal{C}</math>,
* <math>S_g S_h = S_{gh}</math> for all <math>g,h \in G</math> and
* <math>S_g</math> is a [[full and faithful functor]] for every <math>g\in G</math>

we say that <math>(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{S})</math> is a <math>G</math>-graded category.
